clue.text: Old woman going round key or island

indicators.note: something going round another thing travels about its outside, so the old woman ends up either side of what she circles

parts.note: ma = mother, the crossword's stock old woman
alt is a key on every computer keyboard

explanation.walkthrough: 'Key' wants to be the definition — a key is a low sandy island, and the enumeration fits. It is the keyboard sort, and 'or' is only joinery.
explanation.definitionFit: Malta is the Mediterranean island republic south of Sicily, so the definition names it by the geography that gave the country its name.

clue.text: Prominent Communist holding position in African capital

indicators.note: a man holding something keeps it inside his grasp, so the piece named next is enclosed rather than tacked on

parts.note: Mao Zedong, the Communist leader setters reach for when they need three letters
to put something somewhere is to position it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Position' reads as a noun in the surface — a post held in the party — and the wordplay needs it as a verb instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Maputo has been the capital of Mozambique, on the Indian Ocean coast, since independence, which is exactly what the definition asks for.

clue.text: Need a platform — supported by one Conservative associate ineffectually

indicators.note: what supports a thing sits underneath it, and in a down clue underneath means later in the answer

parts.note: to lack something is to need it
the article is taken exactly as it stands
a dais is the low platform a speaker stands on
one = I, the Roman numeral
C is the ballot-paper abbreviation for the Conservative party
an ally is an associate

explanation.walkthrough: Fifteen letters from six ordinary words laid end to end, and nothing is disturbed on the way. The hard part is hearing 'Need' as a verb rather than a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing a thing lackadaisically is doing it listlessly, with no energy or care — which comes to the same as doing it ineffectually.

clue.text: Biblical city with one American subject in region

indicators.note: the bare preposition is the container instruction: what it introduces is dropped inside the region rather than added after it

parts.note: a region is an area; it splits open after its second letter
one = I, the Roman numeral
math is what Americans call the school subject Britons call maths

explanation.walkthrough: 'American subject' looks like it wants a citizen, and the word 'subject' is doing the pointing: it means a subject on the timetable, spelt the American way.
explanation.definitionFit: Arimathea is the town the gospels give as Joseph's home, so the definition points at a place known almost entirely from that one story.

clue.text: Schoolfellow had meal after ship brought in shellfish

indicators.note: bringing something in carries it inside, so the vessel is stowed within the shellfish rather than beside it
in an across clue what comes after follows to the right, so the meal is tacked on at the end

parts.note: a clam is a shellfish, and it opens up after three letters
SS prefixes a steamship's name, as in SS Great Britain
to have had a meal is to have eaten

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is one smooth sentence about supper on the quayside, and the instructions inside it run in a different order from the answer, which is what hides them.
explanation.definitionFit: A classmate is someone taught in the same class, which is what the slightly formal British word schoolfellow names.

clue.text: Demanding to drop target? Hold on

indicators.note: dropping a thing lets it fall away, so the letters named next are simply gone from the longer word

parts.note: someone demanding a right is claiming it
your aim is your target — and these are the three letters that go

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark warns that this is not a sentence about artillery. 'Demanding' is the word to translate first, and everything after it is an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: To cling is to keep a grip and refuse to let go — what the definition's phrasal verb says of a child on a leg or a stubborn habit.

clue.text: A sign outside ranch, home to old car marque

indicators.note: the sign stands on the outside of what follows, wrapping round it instead of sitting beside it

parts.note: the clue's opening word, used as itself

indicators.note: a place that is home to something has it living within, so the abbreviation goes inside the ranch

parts.note: Leo the lion is a sign of the zodiac
a ranch is a farm, opened up after its third letter
o = old, as in OE for Old English

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sign' has half a dozen crossword senses — omen, placard, gesture, symbol — and the zodiac is the one setters use most. The surface's ranch keeps the answer's Italian pedigree out of sight.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfa Romeo is the Milanese car maker, and 'marque' is the trade's word for a manufacturer's badge rather than one of its models.

clue.text: Son sadly getting half twisted in dance

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for son, as in family trees

indicators.note: only half of the sad word is turned round, so its second half is read backwards while the first stays put

parts.note: alas is an exclamation meaning sadly or unfortunately
the second half of the sad word, before turning
the same two letters turned round

explanation.surface: A boy is unhappy at getting tangled up partway through a dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half twisted' is unusual: only the back half of the sad word turns round, while its front half stays where it is.
explanation.definitionFit: Salsa is a lively Latin American dance, as well as the music it is danced to.

clue.text: Crap to animate us immoderately? It's nothing important

indicators.note: to do a thing immoderately is to do it without restraint or proper order, and letters handled that way will not stay as they were given

parts.note: anagram fodder, fifteen letters — exactly the enumeration

explanation.walkthrough: A long anagram sitting in plain sight is the hardest kind to spot, because the fodder reads as an opinion about bad entertainment rather than as a bag of loose letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A storm in a teacup is a great commotion over a trifle, so the idiom names precisely the sort of fuss that turns out to be nothing important.

clue.text: Former partner went to involve court, as anticipated

parts.note: your ex is a former partner

indicators.note: involving someone draws them into what you are already doing, so the abbreviation lands inside rather than after

parts.note: went = peed, the nursery past tense for going to the loo
ct is the standard abbreviation for court in an address

explanation.walkthrough: 'Went' for PEED is a small piece of crossword vocabulary worth storing away: setters use the polite nursery verb whenever those four letters are needed.
explanation.definitionFit: As past participles the two are near-exact synonyms: something anticipated is something looked for in advance, which is what the answer says of an event.

clue.text: Composer recalled trophy given to contralto in Italy

indicators.note: recalled is read as called back, so the trophy word runs backwards

parts.note: a cup is a trophy awarded to a winner
C is a standard abbreviation for contralto in musical scores
I is the international vehicle registration code for Italy

explanation.surface: A cup won by an alto singer in Italy is taken back.
explanation.walkthrough: CUP 'recalled' is PUC, then C, IN and I follow.
explanation.definitionFit: Giacomo Puccini was the Italian opera composer of La Bohème, Tosca and Madama Butterfly.

clue.text: Writer was keenly aware of suggestion

parts.note: to have felt something is to have been keenly aware of it
a tip is a suggestion or hint

explanation.walkthrough: Two words joined and nothing else done to them, so the whole clue turns on 'Writer' — a person in the surface, an implement in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A felt tip is a pen, and 'writer' names it as the thing that writes rather than the person who does — a swap setters make constantly.

clue.text: Sailor embracing one with a crown

indicators.note: an embrace closes arms round what it holds, so the sailor's letters finish up either side of the numeral

parts.note: tar is old slang for a sailor, from the tarpaulin he wore
one = I, the Roman numeral
the article is used as itself

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sailor' is one of the handful of words with a fixed crossword translation, worth learning beside 'worker' for ANT — three letters, always the same three.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiara is the jewelled semicircular headpiece worn by a queen or a bride, so 'crown' defines it by the family of ceremonial headgear it sits in.

clue.text: Rather ancient anger returning in Georgia with scheme falling short

indicators.note: with joins the scheme word on after the Georgia piece
in puts the reversed anger inside the Georgia abbreviation

parts.note: GA is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Georgia

indicators.note: returning means coming back, so the anger word is reversed

parts.note: ire is anger

indicators.note: falling short means the scheme word stops before its last letter

parts.note: a trick is a scheme or ploy

explanation.surface: An old person's temper flares again down in Georgia, and the plan to deal with it comes to nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: IRE 'returning' is ERI, which goes 'in' GA; TRICK 'falling short' is TRIC, added 'with' it.
explanation.definitionFit: Geriatric relates to old age, and is used informally to mean very old or decrepit.

clue.text: Victorian device indicative of changing times?

definitions.meaning: the surface offers nineteenth-century machinery: an engine, a contraption with moving parts
two readings sit here — an era in flux, and the plain business of changing your clothes on a beach

explanation.walkthrough: There is no wordplay to unpick, only a second reading to find: 'changing' is the getting-undressed sort, and the times are Victorian bathing manners rather than history.
explanation.definitionFit: It was a wheeled hut horses towed into the shallows so a swimmer could undress unseen, which makes it a device and squarely of its century.

clue.text: Reminiscences? No way seaweed will grip one

definitions.note: The answer is a mass noun for a feeling, while 'reminiscences' is a plural naming the individual memories that feeling is made of, so the two do not agree in number.

indicators.note: to grip a thing is to close round it, so the seaweed takes the numeral inside itself rather than alongside

parts.note: the word is used exactly as it stands
st = street, the crossword's usual way
a single alga is one seaweed; the plural is algae
one = I, the Roman numeral

explanation.walkthrough: 'No way' is a single exclamation in the surface and two separate pieces in the wordplay, which is where the clue hides. The question mark warns the definition is loose.
explanation.definitionFit: Nostalgia is the wistful longing for the past that reminiscing produces, so the setter names the feeling by the memories people swap when they have it.

clue.text: Bill getting misplaced in sequence? It's due to the cold

indicators.note: in places the jumbled letters inside the sequence word

parts.note: a chain is a connected sequence, as in a chain of events

indicators.note: getting misplaced means ending up in the wrong places, so the letters of Bill are rearranged

explanation.surface: An invoice has been filed out of order in a series, and the chill is blamed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting misplaced' turns BILL into ILBL, which goes 'in' CHAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: A chilblain is a painful itchy swelling on the skin caused by exposure to cold and damp.

clue.text: A pig securing very old record? It's better than average

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it fast inside your grasp, so the pig closes round the letters that follow

parts.note: the clue's first word, used as itself
a boar is a male pig, opened up after two letters
v = very, as in 'v good'
an EP, or extended play, is a record format long out of date

explanation.walkthrough: 'Very old record' looks like one phrase about an antique disc and is really two separate jobs, which is the trap. Everything else is farmyard scenery.
explanation.definitionFit: In everyday speech the phrase means better than usual, though in golf a score above par is the worse one — the idiom keeps the general sense.

clue.text: Vacation inspiring Sayers novel

definitions.meaning: the surface promises an ordinary fortnight away from work
Dorothy L. Sayers took this phrase for a 1937 Lord Peter Wimsey title, swapping its second word for Honeymoon

explanation.walkthrough: There are no letters to assemble: the first word is the definition and the rest is a literary nod, so this is a clue you finish from the crossing letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names time off spent doing the very job you are supposed to be off from, so 'Vacation' gives the category and the joke is in which sort.

clue.text: Central heating smelly, not initially fresh

parts.note: CH is the estate-agent abbreviation for central heating

indicators.note: not initially means without its first letter, so the smelly word loses its opening

parts.note: reeky means smelling strongly and unpleasantly
the first letter of the smelly word

explanation.surface: A room's heating system gives off a pong that is anything but fresh air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fresh' looks like the surface's clean air, but it means impudent, as in getting fresh with someone.
explanation.definitionFit: Fresh can mean impertinent or overfamiliar, which is the same as being cheeky.

clue.text: Be unsteady, being sick during leave

indicators.note: one thing that happens during another falls inside its span, so the illness is placed within the leave

parts.note: to leave a place is to vacate it
sick = ill

explanation.walkthrough: 'Leave' is a noun in the surface — the sick leave you book — and a verb in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To vacillate is to waver between two courses, so the definition catches it as a verb phrase — unsteadiness of mind rather than of the feet.

clue.text: Record company bringing up some imperishable ballad

indicators.note: in a down clue up means from the bottom towards the top, so the buried letters are read backwards
'some' asks for a part of what follows rather than the whole of it, which is how a concealed run of letters is signalled

parts.note: five consecutive letters lie across the join between these two words, running the wrong way

explanation.walkthrough: Long words are the best hiding places because nobody reads across them letter by letter, and the reversal keeps the run invisible even once you start looking.
explanation.definitionFit: A label is the firm that signs musicians and issues their records, so the definition is the music trade's own name for that business.

clue.text: Edition of newspaper — English Times — reflected skill

parts.note: X is the multiplication sign, read as times

indicators.note: reflected means mirrored, so the skill word is reversed

parts.note: art is skill, as in the art of conversation

explanation.surface: A newspaper's edition, featuring an English paper called the Times, shows off its skill.
explanation.walkthrough: E and X are followed by ART 'reflected', TRA. The capital T and the newspaper context make Times look like the London paper; here it is the multiplication sign.
explanation.definitionFit: An extra is a special edition of a newspaper issued outside its normal schedule, often for breaking news.

clue.text: Person who's busy with letters on taps, wooden

definitions.note: The answer is a noun — the tree and its timber — where 'wooden' is an adjective; setters allow a material to be defined by the adjective describing what is made of it.

parts.note: a busy bee is the standing phrase for someone who never stops
British taps are marked C for cold and H for hot

explanation.walkthrough: Taps carry exactly two letters, and spotting that pair is the way in. The comma after 'taps' is where the wordplay stops and the definition begins.
explanation.definitionFit: Beech is the pale hardwood used for chairs, worktops and floors, so the adjective points at the answer as the stuff such things are made from.

clue.text: Activist willing to talk, but losing heart when backing common use of plastic

indicators.note: the heart of a word is the letter at its centre, and losing it takes just that one out
in an across clue backing means the letters travel right to left, the order you would read them in a mirror

parts.note: willing to talk = gabby; the middle letter goes and what is left is turned round
a pol is a politician, chiefly in American usage — the clue's political operator

explanation.walkthrough: Two scraps of unfamiliar vocabulary meet here: 'pol' for a political operator, and 'poly' as the British shortening of polythene that names the thing in every shop.
explanation.definitionFit: A poly bag is the flimsy polythene carrier or wrapper that most plastic ends up as, which is exactly the everyday use the definition describes.

clue.text: Dazed state after consuming hot slice

indicators.note: to consume a thing is to take it in and swallow it, so the letter disappears inside the word rather than following it

parts.note: a dazed state is a trance, opened up before its last letter
h = hot, the letter on the tap

explanation.walkthrough: The surface has somebody eating in a daze, which is a long way from the boardroom and the kitchen where the answer's two everyday senses live.
explanation.definitionFit: Tranche is French for slice and English keeps it for a portion cut off a larger whole, usually of money, shares or debt.

clue.text: Bit of apple glory, cultivated in the style of NZ variety

indicators.note: cultivated means grown and tended, and here the letters are worked into a new order
a bit of a word here is just its first letter

parts.note: the word apple, whose first letter is taken
taken as written, letters to rearrange
a la, from French, means in the style of

explanation.surface: A piece of fruit's splendour, grown in the manner of a New Zealand cultivar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'apple' tempts as the definition, but the variety comes at the end. Royal Gala is an apple variety developed in New Zealand.
explanation.definitionFit: Royal Gala is a sweet apple cultivar that originated in New Zealand, one of its best-known varieties.

clue.text: Feeling cold? Note fast-food shop, not church

parts.note: n = note, the dictionary abbreviation

indicators.note: the bare word is the deletion instruction: whatever it names next is absent from the shop

parts.note: a chippy is a fish-and-chip shop, the British high street's own fast food
ch = church on maps and signposts — these are the letters taken away

explanation.walkthrough: The chip shop carries the joke: strip the church abbreviation off its front and what remains describes the weather you queue in outside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Nippy describes air cold enough to nip at fingers and ears, so the definition names the sensation the weather gives rather than the weather itself.
